propositions.text: Applicants seek judicial review of RAD decision confirming RPD refusal of refugee claim.
propositions.quote: The Applicants seek judicial review of a decision of the Refugee Appeal Division [RAD], dated September 2, 2022, confirming the refusal of their refugee claim by the Refugee Protection Division [RPD].

propositions.text: RPD and RAD concluded Applicants had viable internal flight alternative in Bengaluru, India.
propositions.quote: The RPD and the RAD concluded that the Applicants had a viable internal flight alternative [IFA] in Bengaluru, India

propositions.text: Applicants were neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection under sections 96 and 97 of IRPA.
propositions.quote: and accordingly, that they were neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection under sections 96 and 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA].

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicants seek judicial review of RAD decision confirming RPD refusal, which found a viable internal flight alternative and no refugee protection under IRPA.

propositions.text: Dismissing application as Applicants have not identified a reviewable error.
propositions.quote: For the reasons set out below, I am dismissing the application, as the Applicants have not identified a reviewable error.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application because Applicants have not identified a reviewable error.

propositions.text: Applicants are a married couple from Kerala, India fearing persecution by CPI and Kerala state police.
propositions.quote: The Applicants are a married couple who are citizens of India from the state of Kerala. They claim a fear of persecution at the hands of the Communist Party of India – Marxist [CPI], and the Kerala state police [together, the Agents of Harm].

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicants are a married couple from Kerala fearing persecution by CPI and Kerala police.

propositions.text: Principal Applicant supported Congress Party, witnessed abduction by CPI, reported it, was assaulted and threatened, then relocated within India before coming to Canada.
propositions.quote: The Principal Applicant is a supporter of the Indian National Congress Party [Congress Party]. He witnessed an abduction of a Congress Party member (referred to in the RAD decision as “Shammy”) by CPI while transporting the Congress Party member as part of his job as a taxi driver. The Principal Applicant recognized one of the offenders as a kingpin of the CPI and after the member was found badly beaten, reported the incident to the Congress Party and then to the police. He was subsequently picked up by the police who brought him to members of the CPI who assaulted him and demanded that he retract his police statement. When he did not do so, the CPI began making inquiries at his home and with his family. The Applicants relocated within India shortly thereafter, and lived in another state (Chennai) for three months before coming to Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes the Principal Applicant's political support, witnessing abduction, assault, threats, relocation, and eventual move to Canada.

propositions.text: The determinative issue for RPD and RAD was availability of an internal flight alternative in Bengaluru.
propositions.quote: The determinative issue for both the RPD and the RAD was the availability of an IFA in Bengaluru.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the key issue was whether an internal flight alternative existed in Bengaluru.

propositions.text: RAD found Agents of Harm lacked sufficient motivation to pursue Applicants in IFA and no good grounds to fear future persecution there.
propositions.quote: On the first prong of the IFA test, the RAD found that the Agents of Harm did not have sufficient motivation to pursue the Applicants in the IFA. The RAD found on the reasonable possibility standard that there were no good grounds to fear future persecution in the IFA.

propositions.text: RAD implicitly found Applicants would not face personal risk of torture under section 97 IRPA.
propositions.quote: It also found it implicit that the Applicants would not be subjected to a personal risk of danger of torture under section 97 of the IRPA.

propositions.text: RAD concluded neither section 96 nor 97 of IRPA were satisfied.
propositions.quote: As such, it concluded that neither section 96 nor section 97 had been satisfied.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found no motivation for harm in IFA, no risk of torture, and concluded sections 96 and 97 were not met.

propositions.text: Did RAD err by not conducting independent paragraph 97(1)(a) and (b) analysis?
propositions.quote: Did the RAD err by not conducting an independent paragraph 97(1)(a) and (b) analysis?

propositions.text: Did RAD err in concluding Agents of Harm lacked motivation to pursue Applicants in IFA?
propositions.quote: Did the RAD err in concluding that the Agents of Harm lacked sufficient motivation to pursue the Applicants in the IFA?

propositions.text: Did RAD breach procedural fairness by referring to external evidence not in the record?
propositions.quote: Did the RAD breach procedural fairness by referring to external evidence that was not included in the record?

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies issues: whether RAD erred on section 97 analysis, motivation to pursue, and procedural fairness regarding external evidence.

propositions.text: Standard of review is reasonableness; no rebutting situations present per Vavilov.
propositions.quote: The parties assert and I agree that the standard of review is reasonableness. None of the situations that would rebut the presumption that all administrative decisions are reviewable on a reasonableness standard are present in this case: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 [Vavilov] at paras 16-17 and 25.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the standard of review is reasonableness, with no rebutting factors per Vavilov.

propositions.text: Reasonable decision is internally coherent, rational, justified by facts and law, and shows justification, transparency, intelligibility.
propositions.quote: A reasonable decision is “based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis” and is “justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker”: Vavilov at paras 85-86; Canada Post Corp v Canadian Union of Postal Workers, 2019 SCC 67 at paras 2, 31. A decision will be reasonable if when read as a whole and taking into account the administrative setting, it bears the hallmarks of justification, transparency, and intelligibility: Vavilov at paras 91-95, 99-100.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the reasonableness standard requires coherent, justified, transparent, and intelligible decisions.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness requires applicant knew case and had full chance to respond.
propositions.quote: Questions of procedural fairness ask whether the procedure was fair having regard to all of the circumstances with the ultimate question being whether the applicant knew the case it had to meet and had a full and fair chance to respond: Canadian Pacific Railway Company v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 69 at paras 54, 56.

paragraphs.summary: The court states procedural fairness means the applicant knew the case and had a full chance to respond.

propositions.text: RAD made fatal error by not conducting separate paragraph 97(1)(a) and (b) analysis, citing Paramananthalingam.
propositions.quote: The Applicants argue that the RAD made a fatal error by not conducting a separate paragraph 97(1)(a) and (b) analysis. They refer to the Court’s decision in Paramananthalingam v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 236 [Paramananthalingam], where Justice McVeigh held that it was unreasonable in the context of that case (which did not involve an IFA) that the RPD did not conduct a separate section 97 analysis, after dismissing the applicant’s claim under section 96.

propositions.text: Section 97 protects those with personalized risk of harm even if lacking well-founded fear of persecution under section 96.
propositions.quote: [16] The purpose of section 97 is to capture those legitimate refugee claimants who may not meet the stringent standards of a well-founded fear of persecution. Despite the lower evidentiary threshold under section 96, proving both objective and subjective fear of persecution is very difficult. Section 97 acts as a safety valve which Parliament created to protect those persons who, even if found lacking credibility, face a personalized risk of harm. It bears repeating here that well-founded fear of persecution and a personalized risk of harm require different analysis.

propositions.text: RPD erred by assuming failure under section 96 means failure under section 97 due to higher evidentiary standard.
propositions.quote: [17] The RPD on these facts unreasonably assumes that if the test under section 96 cannot be met, then neither can the test under section 97. According to the RPD, this is due to the higher evidentiary standard under section 97 (balance of probability) than section 96 (serious possibility). What the RPD fails to grasp is that under section 96, the applicant must prove a serious possibility of a well-founded fear of persecution, as opposed to a personalized risk of harm on a balance of probabilities under section 97. To conflate one test with the other is a reviewable error which makes this decision unreasonable.

propositions.text: Officer should have commented on personalized risk under section 97; absence leaves court guessing.
propositions.quote: [18] The officer should have commented, even briefly, on whether the Applicant faced a personalized risk upon returning to Sri Lanka. Having none of this information, this Court is left guessing at why the Applicant does not meet the test under section 97.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue RAD erred by not doing separate section 97 analysis, citing case law that distinguishes section 96 and 97 tests.

propositions.text: Separate section 97 analysis not always required, especially if lack of credibility shown.
propositions.quote: The Applicants acknowledge that the requirement for a separate section 97 analysis, however, is not absolute. In Paramananthalingam, Justice McVeigh noted that a section 97 analysis is not necessary in all cases, particularly where a lack of credibility has been shown: [19] A separate section 97 analysis does not always need to be done.

propositions.text: If claimant lacks credibility, that suffices to dispose claim unless independent credible evidence supports claim.
propositions.quote: The Federal Court of Appeal in Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Sellan, 2008 FCA 381 at paragraph 3, held that: ….where the Board makes a general finding that the claimant lacks credibility, that determination is sufficient to dispose of the claim unless there is independent and credible documentary evidence in the record capable of supporting a positive disposition of the claim.

propositions.text: Claimant bears onus to show independent credible evidence for positive claim disposition.
propositions.quote: The claimant bears the onus of demonstrating there was such evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants acknowledge separate section 97 analysis not always needed, especially if claimant lacks credibility and no independent evidence supports claim.

propositions.text: Where section 97 allegations same as section 96, RAD not obliged to do separate section 97 analysis.
propositions.quote: Similarly, as noted by the Respondent, where allegations and evidence supporting a section 97 claim are the same as those advanced for section 96, the RAD is under no obligation to undertake a second analysis: Kaur v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FC 1379 at para 50.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues no obligation for separate section 97 analysis if claims under sections 96 and 97 are the same.

propositions.text: Kaur principle applied in Ali: no categorical duty for separate section 97 analysis; depends on circumstances.
propositions.quote: The principle set out in Kaur was recently applied by Justice Walker in Ali v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2019 FC 859 [Ali] at paragraphs 43-45 as follows: [43] The Applicants submit that the RPD’s negative credibility findings were not necessarily dispositive of a claim for protection pursuant to section 97 of the IRPA (Kandiah v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2005 FC 181 at paras 14-16). The Respondent submits that there is no obligation for the RPD to conduct an additional section 97 analysis where an applicant’s allegations regarding their section 97 claim are the same as those advanced in their section 96 claim (Kaur at paras 50-51). [44] In Kaur, Chief Justice Crampton held that there is no categorical duty to conduct a separate section 97 analysis in every case (at para 50): [50] The Board is not obliged to conduct a separate analysis under section 97 in each case. Whether it has an obligation to do so will depend on the circumstances of each case (Kandiah v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2005 FC 181 at para 16, 137 ACWS (3d) 604). Where no claims have been made or evidence adduced that would warrant such a separate analysis, one will not be required (Brovina v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2004 FC 635 at paras 17-18, 254 FTR 244; Velez, above at paras 48-51). [45] In the present case, the basis of the Applicants’ claims is fear of persecution in Sudan due to political opinion which is a section 96 nexus. A section 97 analysis by the RPD would have been based on the same facts, allegations and evidence, and would have resulted in the same outcome. The Applicants presented no claims that would warrant a separate section 97 analysis. As stated by Justice Gibson in Kulendrarajah v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2004 FC 79 at paragraph 13 (see also, El Achkar v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 472 at paras 29-32): [13] The sole bases for the principal Applicant's claims are Convention grounds, that is to say, ethnicity and membership in a particular group. Since I am satisfied that the RPD's credibility analysis and analysis of risk to the principal Applicant in Colombo is sufficient to support its conclusion that the principal Applicant is not at risk of persecution based on a Convention ground if she were required to return to Sri Lanka, it follows that she is equally not a person in need of protection because no other ground to support a need of protection other than a Convention ground was advanced on her behalf and the alleged Convention grounds are not sustainable by reason of the credibility finding. While a more extensive explanation for the RPD's conclusion regarding "person in need of protection" in relation to the principal Applicant might well have been desirable, I am satisfied that its absence does not constitute reviewable error.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent cites Ali applying Kaur: no categorical duty for separate section 97 analysis if claims overlap and no new evidence.

propositions.text: RAD found nexus to Convention ground, assessed risk under section 96, found no reasonable possibility of persecution in IFA, implicitly no danger of torture under section 97.
propositions.quote: In doing so, I have concluded that the Appellants do not face a reasonable possibility of future persecution in the IFA, using the Adjei test. Persecution is a broader concept than torture. As such, in concluding that the Appellants do not have good grounds to fear persecution, I have also implicitly concluded that they would not be subjected personally to a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture within the meaning of Article 1 of the Convention Against Torture.

propositions.text: Applicants do not contest IFA concept applies to section 97 danger of torture assessment.
propositions.quote: The Appellants do not contest that the concept of an IFA applies to an assessment of whether an Appellant faces a danger of torture under s. 97 of the IRPA in this case.

propositions.text: Even applying real risk test for torture, Applicants' claims would fail.
propositions.quote: As such, even if I were to apply the “real risk” (“reasonable chance”) test to assess the risk of torture in this case, as the Appellants commend, their claims would still fail.

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found no reasonable possibility of persecution or danger of torture in IFA, and Applicants do not contest IFA applies to section 97.

propositions.text: Respondent asserts no obligation for separate section 97 analysis if section 96 test not met and factual context same; section 97 has higher burden.
propositions.quote: The Respondent asserts that where a refugee claim is based on a nexus and the claimant cannot satisfy the “more than a mere possibility of persecution” test under section 96, the RAD faced with the same factual context is not required to conduct a separate section 97 analysis under the elevated “balance of probabilities” legal threshold of there being a danger of torture, or risk that is “more likely than not”. It asserts that section 97 imposes a higher legal burden of proof than section 96 of the IRPA relying on Li v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2005 FCA 1 [Li].

propositions.text: Factual underpinnings for section 97 allegations tied to section 96 claim, so no separate assessment needed.
propositions.quote: In this case, it argues that the factual underpinnings for the section 97 allegations were tied to the section 96 claim such that there was no separate aspect that needed to be assessed.

paragraphs.summary: Respondent argues no separate section 97 analysis needed if factual basis same and section 96 test not met, citing higher burden under section 97.

propositions.text: Applicants argue severe beating history means separate section 97 concern was strongly argued before RAD.
propositions.quote: The Applicants take issue with this characterization. They assert that as the Principal Applicant was severely beaten, there was a history of torture. As such, they say it was strongly argued before the RAD that there was a separate section 97 concern such that a nexus analysis alone was not sufficient.

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue severe beating history means a separate section 97 concern was strongly argued before RAD.

propositions.text: Applicants did not contest that IFA concept applies to section 97 danger of torture assessment.
propositions.quote: As stated in paragraph 34 of the reasons cited above, the Applicants did not contest that the concept of an IFA applied to the assessment of whether the Applicants would face a danger of torture under section 97 of the IRPA in the IFA.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Applicants did not contest that IFA concept applies to section 97 danger of torture assessment.

propositions.text: First part of IFA test tracks section 97; sections 96 and 97 analyses not always mutually exclusive.
propositions.quote: The first part of the IFA test tracks section 97. Indeed, the RAD titles its analysis of the first prong of the IFA test as an analysis of the “Risk of persecution or s. 97 harm”. However, an analysis of sections 96 and 97 under this part is not always mutually exclusive.

propositions.text: IFA test rationale helpful in assessing risk under section 97; claimant must show risk in every part of country to be removed to.
propositions.quote: As explained in Sadiq v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2021 FC 430 at paragraphs 40 and 43, which was referenced by the RAD: [40] While the IFA test as it has developed in the law of refugee protection has not been imported directly into subsection 97(1) of the IRPA, its underlying rationale is still helpful in assessing a risk of harm under that provision: see Sanchez v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FCA 99 at para 16; and Barragan Gonzalez v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 502 at para 46. In fact, the first part of the IFA test tracks closely paragraph 97(1)(b)(ii) of the IRPA, which provides that, to be a person in need of protection under paragraph 97(1)(b), the claimant must, among other things, personally be at risk in every part of the country to which they would be removed. While not stated expressly in relation to the risk of torture under paragraph 97(1)(a), this risk must also be present in every part of the country to which the claimant would be removed to entitle a claimant to protection on that basis: see Sasha Baglay and Martin Jones, Refugee Law (2nd ed.) (Toronto: Irwin Law, 2017) at 244. The second part of the IFA test is also incorporated into the assessment under subsection 97(1). A claimant can be entitled to protection under this provision even if there is a place where they would not be at risk as long as it is a place to which it would be unreasonable to expect them to relocate. [...] [43] Under the first part of the test, what a claimant must establish to demonstrate that a particular place is not a viable IFA depends on the nature of the claim for protection. If the claimant is seeking protection as a Convention refugee under section 96 of the IRPA, they must establish that they have a well-founded fear of persecution in the proposed IFA. This includes establishing on a balance of probabilities that there is a serious possibility of persecution in the IFA. If the claimant is seeking protection under section 97 of the IRPA, they must establish on a balance of probabilities that they would be personally subject to a risk to life, to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or that there is a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture in the proposed IFA. Obviously these are not mutually exclusive and many claims involve both section 96 and section 97 of the IRPA. This part of the test is simply a reiteration of the burden borne generally by a claimant seeking protection under sections 96 or 97, as the case may be, only now focused specifically on the proposed IFA. See Olusola v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 799 at para 8.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the IFA test tracks section 97 and sections 96 and 97 analyses may overlap, citing case law.

propositions.text: RAD considered future risk from Agents of Harm and political/religious persecution; no factual context missed.
propositions.quote: In its analysis, the RAD considered the future risk to the Applicants given the Principal Applicant’s interactions with the Agents of Harm after the abduction of Shammy, in addition to whether the Applicants’ would face a reasonable possibility of persecution in the IFA arising from their political affiliation or Christian faith. The Applicants have not satisfied me that there is any factual context that the RAD did not consider in its risk analysis.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RAD considered all relevant risk factors and no factual context was overlooked.

propositions.text: RAD decided future risk on reasonable possibility standard and found no good grounds to fear persecution or torture risk under section 97
propositions.quote: the question of future risk was decided on the reasonable possibility standard, it notes that the overall factual finding that there were not good grounds to fear persecution also applied to the question of whether the Applicants would be subjected to personal danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture

propositions.text: RAD considered full factual context and risk but found section 97 threshold not met
propositions.quote: it is implicit from the reasons that the RAD considered the full factual context and risk to the Applicants, but was of the view that the threshold for section 97 had also not been met

propositions.text: RAD acknowledged Applicants' argument to revisit Li decision and burden for section 97 but rejected it
propositions.quote: The RAD acknowledges and considers that Applicants’ argument that the decision in Li should be revisited and whether a different burden should apply to the section 97 analysis. While it does not accept this argument

propositions.text: RAD confirmed Applicants' claims would fail even applying real risk test for torture
propositions.quote: even if it were to “apply the “real risk” (“reasonable chance”) test to assess the risk of torture in this case, as the [Applicants] commend, their claims would still fail

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found no good grounds for persecution or torture risk under section 97, rejected revisiting Li decision, and said claims fail even under real risk test.

propositions.text: A viable IFA finding disposes of section 97 claim where risk analysis done, citing Salman and Balakumar
propositions.quote: a finding of a viable IFA is dispositive of a section 97 claim where a risk analysis has been undertaken: Salman v Canada ... citing Balakumar v Canada

propositions.text: Unlike Paramanathalingam, no reviewable gap in RAD's section 97 analysis here
propositions.quote: Unlike Paramananthalingam, in my view there is no reviewable gap in the RAD’s analysis

propositions.text: RAD considered section 97 but found test not satisfied based on prior risk analysis
propositions.quote: The RAD turned its mind to section 97, but found based on the risk analysis it had already conducted that the test would not be satisfied

propositions.text: First argument by Applicants must fail
propositions.quote: On this basis, the first argument must fail

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no reviewable gap in RAD's section 97 analysis and rejects Applicants' first argument.

propositions.text: RAD concluded Agents of Harm lacked motivation to locate Applicants in IFA
propositions.quote: the RAD concludes that the Agents of Harm lacked sufficient motivation to locate the Applicants in the IFA

propositions.text: RAD based conclusion on: Agents' past 3.5 month inaction in Chennai, lack of motivation to harm Shammy years after abduction, and insufficient evidence of pending prosecution
propositions.quote: It bases this conclusion on a cumulative set of findings, including inter alia: 1) the past behaviour of the Agents of Harm in not pursuing the Applicants for three and a half months in Chennai despite knowing of their presence there; 2) that the Agents of Harm were not motivated to harm Shammy years after the abduction; and 3) that there was insufficient evidence of pending prosecution that would give rise to a continued interest in the Applicants

paragraphs.summary: The RAD found Agents of Harm lacked motivation to pursue Applicants based on past inaction, Shammy's situation, and lack of prosecution evidence.

propositions.text: Applicants challenge each RAD finding and argue Decision is unreasonable
propositions.quote: The Applicants take issue with each of these findings and raise a number of arguments as to why the Decision is unreasonable

propositions.text: Court does not find Applicants' arguments persuasive
propositions.quote: As set out further below, I do not find these arguments persuasive

paragraphs.summary: Applicants challenge RAD findings as unreasonable; court rejects these arguments.

propositions.text: Applicants say RAD unreasonably relied on 3-month Chennai stay and misapplied Ortiz case
propositions.quote: Applicants argue it was unreasonable for the RAD to rely on their three-month stay in Chennai ... RAD’s reference to Ortiz ... is misplaced

propositions.text: Respondent says Ortiz did not set minimum timeframe; RAD could apply its principle to facts here
propositions.quote: Ortiz did not dictate any minimum timeframe for this type of analysis ... It was open for the RAD to refer to Ortiz for the general principle ... and then to apply this principle to the facts of the case

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue RAD unreasonably relied on short stay and misapplied Ortiz; Respondent says Ortiz sets no minimum timeframe and RAD applied principle properly.

propositions.text: RAD relied on Agents' inaction after knowing Applicants were in Chennai and no steps taken to pursue or involve authorities
propositions.quote: the RAD relied not just on the passage of time, but also on the fact that ... once they knew the Applicants were in Chennai they took no steps to pursue them further ... no evidence of steps taken to solicit assistance from the authorities in Chennai

paragraphs.summary: RAD found Agents of Harm took no steps to pursue Applicants after learning their Chennai location, including no authority involvement.

propositions.text: Applicants cite Marimuthu case with different facts involving police detentions and beatings
propositions.quote: Marimuthu involved two incidents where the police detained the applicant ... no further contact was made with the Applicants after the first incident

propositions.text: This case differs from Marimuthu as no further contact occurred after first incident
propositions.quote: In this case, no further contact was made with the Applicants after the first incident when the Agents of Harm learned of the Applicants’ whereabouts

paragraphs.summary: Applicants cite Marimuthu with police detentions; court finds this case differs as no further contact occurred after first incident.

propositions.text: RAD could consider specific factual context in assessing motivation without reviewable error
propositions.quote: it was open for the RAD to consider the specific factual context at play when assessing whether there was motivation to pursue the Applicants in the IFA. Such consideration does not constitute a reviewable error

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD's consideration of factual context in motivation assessment was proper and not erroneous.

propositions.text: Applicants dispute RAD's reliance on Shammy's circumstances to assess risk to Applicants
propositions.quote: Applicants take issue with the RAD’s reliance on the circumstances involving Shammy as informing the risk to the Applicants

propositions.text: RAD upheld RPD's finding that Agents lacked motivation to harm Shammy after kidnapping, so unlikely to harm Applicants
propositions.quote: RAD upheld the RPD’s finding that as the Agents of Harm were not motivated to harm Shammy after he had been kidnapped, it was unlikely that they would be motivated to harm the Applicants

paragraphs.summary: Applicants dispute RAD's reliance on Shammy's situation; RAD upheld finding Agents lacked motivation to harm Shammy or Applicants.

propositions.text: Shammy lived in Kerala 2.5 years after attack; no evidence Agents caused his current incommunicado status
propositions.quote: Shammy lived in Kerala for two and a half years after he was attacked ... no evidence to suggest that the lack of knowledge about his current whereabouts had anything to do with the Agents of Harm

propositions.text: Principal Applicant testified no concern about Shammy's well-being and confidence Communist Party and police would not harm Shammy
propositions.quote: Principal [Applicant] expressed confidence that the Communist Party and police would not harm Shammy anymore

propositions.text: Applicants dispute RAD's summary of evidence about Shammy
propositions.quote: Applicants take some issue with this summary of the evidence

propositions.text: Court finds RAD's summary not a mischaracterization and no evidence Shammy was incommunicado due to Agents
propositions.quote: I do not consider it a mischaracterization ... no evidence to suggest that Shammy was incommunicado because of actions by, or fear of, the Agents of Harm

paragraphs.summary: Shammy lived 2.5 years post-attack; RAD found no evidence Agents caused his incommunicado status; court finds RAD's summary accurate.

propositions.text: RAD reasonably considered Shammy's situation as relevant to motivation; Applicants seek reweighing evidence
propositions.quote: it was reasonable for the RAD to consider what it knew about the situation involving Shammy as a relevant factor when considering motivation. The Applicants’ argument amounts to a request for the Court to reweigh this evidence

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD reasonably considered Shammy's situation; Applicants merely seek reweighing evidence.

propositions.text: Applicants say RAD erred relying on no FIR produced and FIR upload requirement was recent Supreme Court decision
propositions.quote: Applicants assert that the RAD erred in relying on the fact that no FIR was produced ... requirement only stemmed from a decision of the Supreme Court of India that was issued shortly before the abduction of Shammy

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue RAD erred relying on no FIR and that FIR upload requirement was recent Supreme Court decision.

propositions.text: Court agrees with Respondent that FIR use and availability discussed in NDP; RAD's reference reasonable
propositions.quote: I agree with the Respondent, as the use of FIRs to initiate investigations and their availability was discussed in the National Documentation Package [NDP], it was not unreasonable for the RAD to make reference to this tool

propositions.text: Absence of FIR was one factor among others; Applicants did not mention prosecution or trial in claim or letter; Principal Applicant had no evidence for pending prosecution
propositions.quote: reference to the absence of an FIR was only one of the factors ... Applicants did not mention any such prosecution or trial ... Principal Applicant could only state that he thought there was pending prosecution, but could not offer any evidence

paragraphs.summary: Court finds RAD reasonably referenced FIR absence as one factor; Applicants gave no evidence of pending prosecution.

propositions.text: Applicants' remaining arguments are a 'treasure hunt' for error, which is improper in reasonableness review
propositions.quote: The remaining arguments ... can best be described as a treasure hunt for error ... This is not the proper approach for a reasonableness review: Vavilov at para 102

paragraphs.summary: Court finds Applicants' detailed search for error improper under reasonableness review standard.

propositions.text: Court not persuaded that Applicants made viable procedural fairness argument
propositions.quote: With respect to the Applicants’ procedural fairness arguments, I am similarly not persuaded that a viable argument has been made

paragraphs.summary: Court is not persuaded Applicants made a viable procedural fairness argument.

propositions.text: Applicants say certain footnotes reference improper extrinsic evidence
propositions.quote: Applicants point to certain references made in footnotes of the Decision as being references to improper extrinsic evidence

propositions.text: Footnote references relate to information supported in NDP or not material to Decision
propositions.quote: the references relate to information that is either supported within the NDP, and therefore not novel, or is not material to the Decision

paragraphs.summary: Applicants allege improper extrinsic evidence in footnotes; court finds references supported by NDP or immaterial.

propositions.text: Applicants argue RAD breached fairness by citing Kerala police website in footnote
propositions.quote: Applicants argue that the RAD breached procedural fairness by referring to the Kerala police website in a footnote to the Decision

propositions.text: Website cited only to support NDP statements about FIR availability; no procedural unfairness
propositions.quote: the website is not cited to establish new information. Rather, it simply provides further support to statements made in the NDP regarding the availability of FIRs on police websites. I do not consider this reference to create an issue of procedural unfairness

paragraphs.summary: Applicants argue procedural fairness breach by citing police website; court finds citation supports NDP and is fair.

propositions.text: Applicants say RAD cited NDP source about peaceful elections and BJP win, unclear if accurate
propositions.quote: Applicants point to the RAD’s reliance on evidence from the 2011 census relating to the number of Christians in Bengaluru

propositions.text: Unclear if statement about BJP win is in NDP, but statement not material or prejudicial
propositions.quote: While it is unclear whether this specific statement is found in the source from the NDP cited, the specific statement made in the footnote ... is not material to the overall finding and its inclusion does not serve to prejudice the Applicants

paragraphs.summary: Applicants challenge RAD's citation about elections; court finds statement immaterial and not prejudicial.

propositions.text: Court accepts 2011 census info on Christians in Bengaluru as generally recognized fact supported by NDP
propositions.quote: I accept this information in view of its source as a generally recognized fact that is further supported by information in the NDP

propositions.text: Use of generally recognized facts supported by NDP does not amount to unfair extrinsic evidence, citing Aladenika and Wang
propositions.quote: This does not amount to unfair extrinsic evidence: Aladenika v Canada ... Wang v Canada

paragraphs.summary: Court accepts census info as recognized fact supported by NDP; cites precedent that this is not unfair extrinsic evidence.

propositions.text: Applicants have not identified a breach of procedural fairness
propositions.quote: In my view, the Applicants have not identified a breach of procedural fairness

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes Applicants have not shown any procedural fairness breach.

propositions.text: The application will be dismissed for all the reasons given.
propositions.quote: For all of these reasons, the application will be dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application for all the reasons given.

propositions.text: At the hearing, both parties confirmed no question for certification was raised.
propositions.quote: At the hearing of the application, both parties confirmed that they did not have a question for certification.

propositions.text: Applicants initially said no certification question because they argued Paramananthalingam should apply.
propositions.quote: The Applicants asserted that this was because they were simply arguing that Paramananthalingam should apply.

propositions.text: After hearing, Applicants changed position and now seek certification on whether RAD must consider s. 97(1)(a) and (b) if s. 96 was considered.
propositions.quote: He now argues that certification should be ordered on the following question: Does the RAD have to consider s. 97(1)(a) and (b) in relation to the first prong analysis of the Internal Flight Alternative, if s. 96 has been considered?

paragraphs.summary: The court notes parties initially had no certification question; Applicants later seek certification on RAD's consideration of s. 97(1)(a) and (b) after s. 96.

propositions.text: Respondent opposes the Applicants' request for certification.
propositions.quote: The Respondent opposes this request.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent opposes the Applicants' request for certification.

propositions.text: Ali decision does not introduce new propositions beyond those already before the Court.
propositions.quote: I do not view Ali as introducing any new propositions that were not already before the Court when the Applicants’ initial position on certification was made.

propositions.text: Ali paragraphs 43-45 simply refer to and apply the Court’s decision in Kaur, which was already before the Court.
propositions.quote: Paragraphs 43-45 of Ali, which are cited above, simply refer and apply the Court’s decision in Kaur, which was already before the Court.

propositions.text: Applicants assert their change in position is due to Ali decision.
propositions.quote: While counsel for the Applicants asserts that this change in position is a result of Ali,

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Ali does not add new propositions; Applicants say their change is due to Ali, but Ali only applies Kaur already before the Court.

propositions.text: The court will not entertain the Applicants' change in position and denies the certification request.
propositions.quote: In my view, this change in position cannot be entertained. Accordingly, the request is denied.

propositions.text: The judicial review application is dismissed and no question of general importance is certified.
propositions.quote: The application for judicial review is dismissed. No question of general importance is certified.

paragraphs.summary: The court denies the Applicants' changed certification request and dismisses the judicial review application without certifying any question.
